items.title: Clark Terry interviewed by Joe Williams and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, May 19, 1995
items.q: he’d play a little bit with Jo Jones and Walter Page or Freddie and The Fiddler

ctx.x: I know he cracked up, he laughed.

Ever since then, every time we played [scats], Sweets would stand up and take his big solo. But I’ll tell you about this cat, Basie, he, although Ellington was more endowed with harmony and theory and so forth, Basie was the king of mother wit as far as tempo, and he taught us all the greatest lesson in the world and that is the utilization of space and time. All the musicians in the world, and they say he learned it through the medium of just socializing at Kansas City at the Cherry Blossom and the little places…

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I did work in the band for a while with Papa Jo, and of course on many other occasions I worked with Jo: studios – jazz studio gigs and record sessions and so forth.

ctx.x: When you were in the band, did you have an opportunity to play with the rhythm section that had Walter Page and Jo Jones in it, and Freddie Green, or not?

No. Walter Page had long since been out of the band when I – of course I did work in the band for a while with Papa Jo, and of course on many other occasions I worked with Jo: studios – jazz studio gigs and record sessions and so forth. But I never worked with Big Walter Page.
What was Jo Jones, Freddie Green, that rhythm section like to play with in the first band, when you first got there?
